deep.reconstruction:
This page has no mathematics. It is a short practical note, written in faint pencil (probably later than the ink tables on the facing page), recording the dimensions of a glass case for an instrument made by Oertling. Oertling was a Berlin instrument maker; his firm made precision balances and other apparatus.

Heading: 'Dimensionen des Glaskastens zu Oertlings Gon…' ('Dimensions of the glass case for Oertling's …'). The last word is cut off or illegible at the page edge, so the instrument cannot be identified with certainty.

Measurements:
- Tiefe (depth) = 336 mm
- Höhe (height) = 455 mm
- Breite (width) = 496 mm
- Schranktiefe (depth of the cabinet or cupboard meant to hold it) = 348 mm, followed by a '+'. The '+' probably means 'somewhat more than 348 mm' or marks a checked item.

The evident purpose (my inference) is to check that the glass case fits into the cupboard: 348 − 336 = 12 mm of spare depth.

So the computation is just a comparison of lengths. If one wants a derived quantity, the case's volume is 336·455·496 = 75,828,480 mm³, about 75.8 litres (my addition; it is not on the page).

Context: the previous page is Gauss's 1815 reduction table for Polaris at upper culmination. It uses sin(x/2) = s·cosφ·cosδ·sin²(h/2)/sin(A + x/2) and tabulates corrections against hour angle. The next page is a 1816 correspondence log (Olbers, Bessel, Lindenau, Gerling, Encke, etc.). Neither connects to this note, which is an isolated laboratory/household memorandum.
